_readme: Verified findings for the 'chess science' explainer reels. Every number on screen comes from here, never from the model. Keep claims conservative; 'about' is better than a precise figure we are not sure of. Fields: hook (<=7 words, on screen + first spoken words), moment (relatable scene), myth, mechanism, stat (grid/bars), study (who, where, how many), result (bar chart), method (what to do; board step kind from lesson_anim), takeaway, share (send this to the friend who...), sources.

facts.topic: Masters don't have a better memory. They have more patterns.

moment.narration: You see a position for five seconds. Then it's gone. A master sees it once... and rebuilds it.

myth.narration: And no, it's not because masters have a photographic memory.
myth.label: NOT MEMORY

mechanism.narration: Their brain doesn't store pieces. It stores patterns: whole groups of pieces that belong together.
mechanism.label: PATTERNS, NOT PIECES

stat.narration: Show a real game position for five seconds. A master puts back about sixteen of twenty-five pieces. A beginner, about four.
stat.title: PIECES RECALLED OF 25

study.narration: Then the experiment flipped: random positions, pieces scattered with no logic. The master's advantage vanished. Both remembered about three.
study.title: RANDOM POSITIONS

result.narration: Same brain. Same memory. The difference was a library of patterns built from thousands of positions.
result.title: A MASTER'S RECALL

method.narration: So the way to see more is simple: solve real positions every day and let the patterns pile up.
method.label: ONE PATTERN A DAY

takeaway.narration: Your memory is fine. Your pattern library just needs daily deposits.
takeaway.label: BUILD THE LIBRARY

facts.share: Send this to the friend who says they have a bad memory for chess
sources: de Groot, Thought and Choice in Chess (1946/1965)
Chase & Simon, Perception in chess, Cognitive Psychology (1973)

facts.topic: Solo study predicts rating better than playing.
facts.hook: Playing more won't raise your rating

moment.narration: Another blitz game. And another. And another. Your rating... exactly where it was last month.

myth.narration: And no, the problem isn't that you need to play more.
myth.label: NOT MORE GAMES

mechanism.narration: A game tests what you already know. Serious study is where new patterns actually get built.
mechanism.label: GAMES TEST. STUDY BUILDS.

stat.narration: Researchers tracked hundreds of tournament players and logged how they spent their chess time.
stat.label: TOURNAMENT PLAYERS
stat.title: HOW THEY SPENT THEIR TIME

study.narration: The strongest predictor of rating wasn't games played. It was hours of serious study alone.
study.title: WHAT PREDICTS RATING

result.narration: In their first ten years, future masters had put in about five thousand hours of solo study. Intermediate players, about one thousand.
result.title: HOURS OF SOLO STUDY

method.narration: Solo study doesn't mean hours. It means minutes with full focus: a position, candidates, calculate, check.
method.label: TEN FOCUSED MINUTES

takeaway.narration: Play for fun. Study to improve. Ten focused minutes a day beats fifty blitz games.
takeaway.label: STUDY BEATS BLITZ

facts.share: Send this to the friend who plays 50 blitz games a day
sources: Charness, Tuffiash, Krampe, Reingold & Vasyukova, The role of deliberate practice in chess expertise, Applied Cognitive Psychology (2005)

facts.topic: The air in the room changes how many mistakes you make.
facts.hook: The air is making you blunder

moment.narration: Round three of the tournament. Stuffy hall, a hundred players, windows shut. And your calculation starts to slip.

myth.narration: And no, it's not just tiredness.
myth.label: NOT JUST TIRED

mechanism.narration: Tiny particles in the air reach the brain and quietly degrade decision-making, especially under time pressure.
mechanism.label: FINE PARTICLES, FOGGY MOVES

stat.narration: Economists put air sensors inside real chess tournaments in Germany and ran every move through an engine.
stat.label: MOVES CHECKED BY ENGINE
stat.title: SENSORS IN THE PLAYING HALL

study.narration: Same players, same tournament. On days with worse air, the chance of a mistake went up by about two percentage points.
study.title: CHANCE OF AN ERROR

result.narration: And the mistakes themselves got about eleven percent bigger. Under time pressure, the effect was even stronger.
result.title: SIZE OF THE MISTAKES

method.narration: You can't control the hall. You can control your time: calculate the forcing moves early, before the clock gets low.
method.label: DON'T GET LOW ON TIME

takeaway.narration: Open a window when you train. And train calculation so time pressure never decides your game.
takeaway.label: AIR + TIME

facts.share: Send this to the friend who blames every loss on bad luck
sources: Künn, Palacios & Pestel, Indoor Air Quality and Cognitive Performance, Management Science (2023; IZA DP 2019)

facts.topic: You are not too old to improve.
facts.hook: You're not too old for chess

moment.narration: You're thirty-something, you discover chess, and someone tells you: too late, this is a kids' game.

myth.narration: And no, chess skill does not peak at twenty.
myth.label: NOT A KIDS' GAME

mechanism.narration: Chess runs on two engines: raw calculation, which fades slowly, and pattern knowledge, which keeps growing for decades.
mechanism.label: SPEED FADES, KNOWLEDGE GROWS

stat.narration: Researchers analysed one point six million moves from about four thousand professional players, across one hundred and twenty-five years of games.
stat.label: 4,000 PLAYERS · 1.6M MOVES
stat.title: 125 YEARS OF CHESS

study.narration: Move quality kept improving through the twenties and thirties.
study.title: MOVE QUALITY BY AGE

result.narration: Performance peaked around age thirty-five, and stayed on that plateau until about forty-five.
result.title: RELATIVE PERFORMANCE

method.narration: The engine that grows with age is patterns. Feed it: one real position a day, calculated to the end.
method.label: FEED THE PATTERN ENGINE

takeaway.narration: Starting at thirty is not late. It's a fifteen-year climb that hasn't begun.
takeaway.label: THE CLIMB STARTS NOW

facts.share: Send this to the friend who thinks they started chess too late
sources: Strittmatter, Sunde & Zegners, Life cycle patterns of cognitive performance over the long run, PNAS (2020)

facts.topic: Your first good idea blocks a better one.
facts.hook: Your first idea is blocking you

moment.narration: You spot a mate in five. Beautiful. You play it. The engine shows a mate in three you never saw.

myth.narration: And no, you didn't miss it because you calculated badly.
myth.label: NOT BAD CALCULATION

mechanism.narration: Once a familiar idea lights up, your eyes keep returning to its squares, even while you think you're searching.
mechanism.label: THE FIRST IDEA HIJACKS YOUR EYES

stat.narration: Researchers gave strong players a position with a familiar five-move mate... and a hidden three-move mate.
stat.title: STRONG PLAYERS TESTED

study.narration: Eye tracking caught it: players said they were looking for better options. Their eyes stayed on the familiar solution.
study.title: WHERE THE EYES WENT

result.narration: Most missed the shorter mate. In that moment they played like players several rating classes weaker.
result.title: EFFECTIVE STRENGTH

method.narration: The fix is a habit: found a good move? Write it down, then look at the board like it's new. Every check, every capture.
method.label: GOOD MOVE? LOOK AGAIN

takeaway.narration: When you see a good move, look for a better one. Lasker said it. Science proved it.
takeaway.label: LOOK FOR A BETTER ONE

facts.share: Send this to the friend who plays the first move they see
sources: Bilalić, McLeod & Gobet, Why good thoughts block better ones: the mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung effect, Cognition (2008)

moment.narration: Two hours of chess videos tonight. You understood everything. Next game... you remember nothing.

myth.narration: And no, you don't need to watch it again.
myth.label: NOT REWATCHING

mechanism.narration: Memory isn't built when information goes in. It's built when you pull it back out.
mechanism.label: RECALL BUILDS MEMORY

stat.narration: In a classic experiment, students learned a text. One group re-read it. The other group was tested on it instead.
stat.label: STUDENTS
stat.title: RE-READ vs RECALL

study.narration: Right away, both groups looked similar. The re-readers even felt more confident.
study.title: AFTER 5 MINUTES

result.narration: One week later, the re-readers kept forty percent. The group that practised recall kept sixty-one percent.
result.title: REMEMBERED AFTER ONE WEEK

method.narration: So don't watch the solution. Cover it, list the checks and captures, commit to a move, and only then check.
method.label: COMMIT BEFORE YOU CHECK

takeaway.narration: A puzzle you solve is worth ten you watch.
takeaway.label: SOLVE, DON'T WATCH

facts.share: Send this to the friend who watches chess videos instead of training
sources: Roediger & Karpicke, Test-enhanced learning, Psychological Science (2006)

facts.topic: How long until training becomes automatic.
facts.hook: Why your chess habit keeps dying

moment.narration: Day one: motivated. Day four: tired. Day nine: you forgot chess existed.

myth.narration: And no, it's not a willpower problem.
myth.label: NOT WILLPOWER

mechanism.narration: A habit forms when a cue and an action repeat until the brain stops needing a decision.
mechanism.label: CUE → ACTION → REPEAT

stat.narration: Researchers followed ninety-six people building a new daily habit and measured when it became automatic.
stat.label: PEOPLE
stat.title: BUILDING A DAILY HABIT

study.narration: On average it took sixty-six days. Some needed eighteen. Some needed over two hundred.
study.title: DAYS TO AUTOMATIC

result.narration: And missing a single day made almost no difference. What killed habits was stopping for good.
result.title: DAMAGE TO THE HABIT

method.narration: Make it tiny and fixed: same time, one puzzle, every day. The streak is the cue.
method.label: SAME TIME, ONE PUZZLE

takeaway.narration: Motivation gets you to day four. A streak gets you to day sixty-six.
takeaway.label: GET TO DAY 66

facts.share: Send this to the friend who restarts their chess training every Monday
sources: Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts & Wardle, How are habits formed, European Journal of Social Psychology (2010)

facts.topic: Fast games multiply blunders, even for grandmasters.

moment.narration: Thirty seconds on the clock. You see the move, you grab the piece... and you've just hung your queen.

myth.narration: And no, it's not because you're bad under pressure.
myth.label: NOT A NERVES PROBLEM

mechanism.narration: With less time, you skip the one step that catches blunders: checking your opponent's reply.
mechanism.label: THE SKIPPED STEP

stat.narration: Researchers ran thousands of grandmaster moves through an engine, from slow games and from rapid games.
stat.label: GRANDMASTER MOVES
stat.title: SLOW vs RAPID

study.narration: In slow games the grandmasters made about five serious mistakes per thousand moves.
study.title: BIG MISTAKES PER 1,000 MOVES

result.narration: In rapid games, about seven. Same players, same brains, about forty percent more blunders.
result.title: BLUNDER RATE

method.narration: The antidote is a reflex you train slowly: before every move, what is their best reply? Checks, captures, threats.
method.label: THEIR BEST REPLY FIRST

takeaway.narration: Blitz doesn't train the blunder check. Slow puzzles do. Then the reflex shows up in blitz.
takeaway.label: TRAIN SLOW, PLAY FAST

facts.share: Send this to the friend who hangs pieces in time trouble
sources: Chabris & Hearst, Visualization, pattern recognition, and forward search: effects of playing speed and sight of the board on grandmaster chess errors, Cognitive Science (2003)

facts.topic: Masters and amateurs use different parts of the brain.

moment.narration: Same position, same clock. The amateur is thinking hard. The master already knows.

myth.narration: And no, the master is not calculating faster.
myth.label: NOT FASTER THINKING

mechanism.narration: Scans showed amateurs lighting up the medial temporal lobe, the region for new information. Masters lit up the frontal and parietal cortex, where stored patterns live.
mechanism.label: RECALL vs FIGURE OUT

stat.narration: Twenty players, from amateur to grandmaster, played matches against a computer while their brain activity was measured.
stat.label: PLAYERS SCANNED
stat.title: AMATEURS TO GRANDMASTERS

study.narration: The stronger the player, the more the activity shifted from working things out to recognising them.
study.title: PATTERN RECALL ACTIVITY

result.narration: Expertise isn't thinking harder. It's recognising more.
result.title: WHERE A MASTER'S BRAIN WORKS

method.narration: You build recognition by meeting patterns again and again: a pin today, a fork tomorrow, until your brain stops computing them.
method.label: MEET THE PATTERN AGAIN

takeaway.narration: Every puzzle you solve moves one more pattern from 'figure out' to 'just know'.
takeaway.label: FROM THINK TO KNOW

facts.share: Send this to the friend who thinks masters just calculate faster
sources: Amidzic, Riehle, Fehr, Wienbruch & Elbert, Pattern of focal gamma-bursts in chess players, Nature (2001)

facts.topic: Masters don't calculate deeper. They calculate better.

moment.narration: You calculate seven moves deep, pick a line... and lose to something on move two.

myth.narration: And no, the answer isn't calculating even deeper.
myth.label: NOT DEEPER

mechanism.narration: When a famous psychologist made players think aloud, masters and club players searched about as deep. The difference was the FIRST moves they looked at.
mechanism.label: BETTER CANDIDATES, SAME DEPTH

stat.narration: Grandmasters, including a world champion, and club players solved the same positions, talking through every thought.
stat.label: PLAYERS, THINKING ALOUD
stat.title: THE THINK-ALOUD STUDY

study.narration: The masters' first candidate was usually already the best move. The club players spent their time on moves that were never going to work.
study.title: FIRST CANDIDATE = BEST MOVE

result.narration: Depth was similar. Quality of the candidates was the whole difference.
result.title: MASTER vs CLUB

method.narration: Before you calculate anything, list the forcing moves: every check, every capture, every threat. Then calculate only those.
method.label: FORCING MOVES FIRST

takeaway.narration: Don't go deeper. Start from better moves.
takeaway.label: START FROM BETTER MOVES

facts.share: Send this to the friend who calculates ten moves deep and still loses
sources: de Groot, Thought and Choice in Chess (1946/1965)

facts.topic: A master knows about fifty thousand patterns.

moment.narration: The master glances at the board and plays instantly. You've been staring for three minutes.

myth.narration: And no, that glance is not talent.
myth.label: NOT TALENT

mechanism.narration: Every position the master has studied left a chunk in memory. The glance is a lookup, not a calculation.
mechanism.label: A LOOKUP, NOT A CALCULATION

stat.narration: Researchers estimated how many chunks a master needs to perform like a master. The answer: around fifty thousand.
stat.label: × 100 = 50,000 PATTERNS
stat.title: A MASTER'S LIBRARY

study.narration: That's roughly the vocabulary of a language. Nobody is born with it. It's collected, one pattern at a time.
study.title: PATTERNS KNOWN

result.narration: One pattern a day is three hundred and sixty-five a year. The library grows whether you feel it or not.
result.title: ONE PATTERN A DAY

method.narration: Don't just solve. Name the pattern after each puzzle: pin, fork, back rank. The name is the label on the shelf.
method.label: NAME THE PATTERN

takeaway.narration: Talent is a library you haven't filled yet.
takeaway.label: FILL THE LIBRARY

facts.share: Send this to the friend who says chess is all talent
sources: Simon & Gilmartin, A simulation of memory for chess positions, Cognitive Psychology (1973)

facts.topic: Chess and school: what the research really shows.
facts.hook: What chess does to a kid's math

moment.narration: Your kid is obsessed with chess. Part of you wonders if those hours should go to homework.

myth.narration: And no, chess doesn't magically make kids geniuses, so let's look at what it actually does.
myth.label: NOT MAGIC

mechanism.narration: Chess trains the same muscles math uses: holding steps in your head, checking before acting, finishing a calculation.
mechanism.label: THE SAME MUSCLES

stat.narration: A meta-analysis pooled twenty-four studies on chess instruction in schools.
stat.label: STUDIES POOLED
stat.title: CHESS IN SCHOOLS

study.narration: Across them, kids who received chess instruction improved in mathematics, with a moderate but real effect.
study.title: MATH RESULTS

result.narration: The effect was clearest for math and problem solving, smaller elsewhere. And it works best when the training is regular, not occasional.
result.title: WHEN IT WORKS

method.narration: Regular means short and daily: one position, calculate to the end, check the answer. Ten minutes.
method.label: TEN MINUTES, DAILY

takeaway.narration: Those chess hours aren't stolen from homework. Ten daily minutes of calculation are homework.
takeaway.label: CHESS IS HOMEWORK

facts.share: Send this to the parent who wonders if chess is worth it
sources: Sala & Gobet, Do the benefits of chess instruction transfer to academic and cognitive skills? A meta-analysis, Educational Research Review (2016)
